permitName: Joshua Tree National Park Wilderness Backpacking Permits

description.cancellation_policy:
Cancellation Policy

The $6.00 reservation fee is 100% non-refundable, including for cancellations made prior to the 24 hour cancellation window. Under no circumstances will a refund be given for a cancelled, modified, or completed permit.

 

Change Policy

  • Changes may be made to your reservation, including exit date, entry/exit locations, designated site selection, and zone selections as late as one day prior to your permitted entry date. No follow up is required with park staff. 
  • To change an entry date, you must cancel the permit and reserve a new permit. All fees apply.  
  • One alternate trip leader may be designated at the time of reservation. The trip leader and alternate trip leader may not be changed and must be present for the permit to be valid.  
  • Campsites along the Boy Scout Trail and camping within the Pine City Backcountry Zone are limited and likely to be competitive. Please be courteous and notify the park as soon as possible if you decide not to use your reservation.
description.comment_box_description: Please provide a detailed trip itinerary below, including both approximate camping locations as well as trails or routes you intend to use. Be as specific as possible! This information helps us better manage park resources and in the event of an emergency, will be used to help locate you. Example: I will hike the Boy Scout Trail starting at Key’s West on Fri., March 24th and exiting at Indian Cove Sat., March 25th at noon. We are camping at site #13. We plan to make a side trip to Willow Hole.
description.description:
Joshua Tree National Park is a vast wilderness covering more than 792,000 acres of the Mojave and Colorado Deserts in Southern California. Of this approxiately 1200 square miles, roughly 85% is managed as wilderness. Ranging in elevation from less than 1000 ft at the park’s eastern boundary to over 5800 ft atop Quail Mountain in the heart of the Little San Bernardino Mountains, this park offers a variety of landscapes and unparalleled opportunities for unconfined, primitive recreation. Higher elevation sites offer sweeping vistas of steep canyons and rocky, exposed summits, expansive Joshua tree and juniper woodlands, as well as the park’s famous monzogranite outcroppings dotted with pinyon pine. Lower elevation sites along the eastern margin of the park offer the opportunity to study vast landscapes of playas, washes, sloping bajadas, and microphyll woodlands. The immense depth of geologic time is visible in the formation of desert varnish on long-exposed rock faces and in small cryptobiotic soil crusts tenaciously clinging to life in the bottom of vast sandy basins.   

Overnight, wilderness backpacking can be accessed from any of 13 backcountry trailheads scattered throughout the park [Wilderness Backpacking ]. These trailheads are accessible through a network of paved and unpaved roads. Most of these areas are accessible by paved roads, although high clearance 4x4 vehicles are needed to access Upper Covington, Geology Tour Road, and Pleasant Valley backcountry trailheads. Roads may be temporarily impassible due to flooding or snow. 

The park is divided into 13 backcountry zones . When making your online reservation, please indicate the zone in which you intend to camp each night. Boy Scout Trail is the only zone in which it is required to camp in designated sites. If planning to only hike the Boy Scout Trail and not enter other zones, please select a specific designated site along the Boy Scout Trail. In contrast, parking locations are designated under entry/exit point during the check out process and should match one of the 13 backcountry trailheads, unless entering the wilderness from outside the park boundary (e.g. along CA-62 east of Twentynine Palms). 

Cell service is spotty or unavailable throughout much of the park, and visitors should carry alternative forms of communication (spot devices) and make all necessary phone calls before entering the park. Potable water is available at Cottonwood Campground, Park Headquarters and the Joshua Tree National Park Visitor Center (in Twentynine Palms), Black Rock Nature Center (Yucca Valley), Indian Cove Ranger Station, and the West Entrance. Gas and other services are not available anywhere inside the park and may be obtained in the towns of Twentynine Palms (outside the north Entrance), Joshua Tree and Yucca Valley (outside West Entrance), or Indio (outside the South Entrance). Although distances may appear short on the map, it can take up to two hours by road to travel across the park.
description.discounts:
No discounts will be given on backcountry permits, including for Senior Annual / Lifetime, and Access pass holders. 

Backcountry permit holders are required to pay all park entrance fees. For general park entry, all discounts and passes will be honored. For a full listing of entrance fees, passes, and discounts, please see the park's Fees & Passes webpage.
description.driving_directions:
Joshua Tree National Park lies within a few hours drive from several major metropolitan areas. The park is located approximately 140 miles east of Los Angeles, 175 miles northeast of San Diego, and 215 southwest of Las Vegas, Nevada. You can approach the park from Interstate 10 (South Entrance) or California Highway 62 (29 Palms Highway) (North or West Entrances).  

  • Please do not rely on GPS directions to navigate to or within Joshua Tree National Park. Navigation systems can route you onto backcountry roads with ruts, rocks, or soft sand that will be impassable to your vehicle. Attempting to use these roads without proper training and / or equipment may result in personal injury or damage to your vehicle.  
  • There is one permit office serving Joshua Tree National Park:
    • Joshua Tree National Park Permit Office, 74485 Twentynine Palms, CA, 92277, Building 100. 
    • This office is located at Park Headquarters, directly across the breezway from the old Oasis of Mara Visitor Center.
  • For further information on how access our park visitor centers, please view our website. 
  • For further directions on how to access Joshua Tree National Park, please refer to our park website.
description.fee_policy:
• There is a $6.00 non-refundable reservation fee for all wilderness backpacking permit reservations in Joshua Tree National Park. 
  • One wilderness backpacking permit is valid for 1-12 people. Group sizes of over 12 are prohibited, unless specifically approved by the permitting office. 
  • All commercial user groups are required to follow the same guidelines as non-commerical users. 
  • All payments must be made electronically through Recreation.gov. In-person payments by credit/debit card only will be accepted at the permit office for same day and advanced permit reservations. Cash payments are not accepted. Payments cannot be made over the phone.
description.need_to_know_email:
• No campfires are allowed anywhere in the backcountry  
  • Camp stoves are allowed 
  • Do not use rock shelters for camping, fires, or toilets  
  • Excrement can be buried in “cat holes” 6-8 inches deep and cannot be in or near rock shelters or outcrops 
  • All trash and toilet paper must be packed out  
  • Camping in day use areas is prohibited 
  • Backpacking must take place one mile from backcountry trailheads, at least a half mile from legally open roads, and at least 200 feet from designated trail  
  • Group size limit for day and overnight use is 12 people 
  • A printed copy or electronic image of your permit must be accessible for inspection by a park representative 
  • Food and water caches are allowed for up to 14 days and must be marked with your name and dates of intended use and must be packed in a hard sided, animal-resistant container 
  • Remove ALL caches at the conclusion of your trip. Expired water caches will be removed by park staff 
  • Parking within the park for backpacking is restricted to backcountry trailheads 
  • Review public land agency rules when parking outside of the park 
  • Natural and cultural resources must be left where found 
  • When possible, hike on trails, rock expanses, or in washes to prevent destruction of cryptobiotic soils and soil compaction 
  • Pets are not allowed on backpacking trails to protect both your pet and wildlife 
  • Service animals are not subject to the park’s pet policies and, when accompanying an individual with a disability, they are allowed wherever visitors are allowed 
  • It is recommended to carry a map, compass, and first-aid kit 
  • Cell phone service is unavailable in most areas. It is recommended to let a friend/family member know of your travel plan and carry a satellite communication device  
  • If you carry an emergency signaling device, know its operation, limitations, and frequency of failure to transmit. If you activate the emergency help function on the device, understand the consequences of what you may be asking of rescue personnel

description.need_to_know_permit:
Download the NPS app prior to visiting the park – trail maps and more!

You are responsible for knowing and abiding by all park rules and regulations and your own safety! Plan and Prepare! 

  • Wilderness travel carries inherent risk. Understand the limitations of your group when planning a wilderness backpacking trip. The park’s backcountry is rugged and subject to adverse weather conditions. 

  • Permit holders are required to carry a digital or printed copy of their permit or confirmation email at all times. 

  • Wilderness backpacking is limited to 3 consecutive nights within a specific campsite or backcountry camping zone and may not exceed 14 days within a season.

  • There is a 30-day camping limit each year.

  • A park entrance pass [physical or digital; Park Passes ] is required to access all backcountry trailheads, unless parking outside of the park. If starting your trip outside the park (i.e. to access the Coxcombs), please contact public lands agencies responsible for those areas.  

Planning and Registration Process 

  • Watch the required video in order to minimize your impact during your trip. Please consider your group’s skill level and experience in desert conditions. For questions or help planning, contact the Joshua Tree National Park permit office at (760) 367-5554. 

  • Review the zoning map and trails associated with each zone. To help rangers respond in emergency, PLEASE INCLUDE YOUR ITINERARY IN THE COMMENTS BOX. Many zones do not have maintained trails, however wilderness backpacking is allowed off trail. Camping regulations of 1 mile from any backcountry trailhead, 0.5 miles from any road, and 200 feet off any trail apply in all areas of the park unless camping along Boy Scout Trail in a designated site. Camping in day use areas is prohibited.

  • During check out, the entry/exit selections are where you will park your vehicle, i.e. the name of the Backcountry Trailhead. These are not the zones in which you intend to camp. See here for assistance.    

  • Once you confirm your trip through Recreation.gov, you will receive a confirmation email with your trip details. Based on staff availability, you may receive a follow-up phone call following completion of your reservation on Recreation.gov 

  • Violations are subject to citation and may result in your permit being revoked.

Vehicles and Parking Information

  • No parking permit is required for vehicles parked overnight at one of the 13 backcountry trailheads. Vehicles are limited to 2 per permit. Parking vehicles at two different parking areas for the same trip is allowed. 

  • Certain parking areas are limited both in terms of the number of available spaces and vehicle size. Please be considerate of other visitors when planning your trip.

  • Improperly parked vehicles (blocking roadways or on top of vegetation) may be subject to citation or towed at owner’s expense.  

Food and Water Storage

  • Water is the limiting factor for any trip in JTNP. When surface water exists, it is reserved for park wildlife. Please carry or cache all water you plan to use.

  • All caches must be marked with name, contact information (phone number / email), and dates of intended use. 

  • Caches must be removed at the conclusion of your trip. Use sturdy containers which cannot be easily damaged by park wildlife. 

  • Food must always be stored properly when not attended. 

  • Although bears are not a concern, smaller animals such as mice, ravens, and coyotes are known to try to access human food and water caches. 

  • Human food is harmful to wildlife and habituated animals are at greater risk of becoming aggressive or being killed. Although not required, please consider carrying food in a wildlife-proof storage container such as a bear bin. 

Human Waste

  • Human waste must be buried in “cat holes” six to eight inches deep and at least 200 feet away from water sources. Do not bury human waste under rocks or in alcoves. 

  • Pack out used toilet paper. Do not leave used toilet paper or exposed excrement in the backcountry.
description.no_show_policy:
Due to the nature of the backcountry at Joshua Tree National Park, it is impractical to monitor arrival and departure of the vast majority of permit holders.  

However, along the Boy Scout Trail, reservations may be cancelled if the permitted party has not occupied their designated campsite along the Boy Scout Trail within 24 hours after scheduled arrival date for multiple day reservations. 

Please be courteous to other visitors and cancel your reservation if you know that you will be unable to make it.
description.quota_details:
Backpacking is limited along the Boy Scout Trail and in the Pine City Zone in order to minimize impacts on the park’s resources in heavily used areas. In all other zones, there is no quota for advanced reservations.  

Boy Scout Trail Designated Sites

  • Accessible from the Indian Cove or Boy Scout Backcountry Trailheads.
  • Camping is limited to one campsite per group along this trail.
  • Group size limitation is campsite specific. Information on size limitations for each of the campsites may be found under “site details” when making your reservation. 
  • Please be considerate of other groups when making a reservation. Please reserve a campsite that is appropriate for your group (i.e. do not book a large site for a small group).   
  • Same day reservations subject to availabity.

Pine City Backcountry Camping Zone

  • Accessible from the Pine City Backcountry Trailhead  
  • Two permits can be obtained in advance through Recreation.gov. Two same day permits are available at Park Headquarters or through Recreation.gov
description.season_information:
Permits are required for ALL overnight, wilderness backpacking trips. Day-use visitors do not need to register.       

  • Online same day permits will be available through recreation.gov up until 11:59pm on the day of departure. In person same day permits will be available up until 4pm at the permit office located at 74485 National Park Blvd, Twentynine Palms, CA, 92277, Bldg. 100; Everyday, 8:00am - 4:00pm. Permits may be subject to change based on demand and staff availability.
  • Permits for all zones, including Boy Scout Trail designated sites, can be obtained up to 6 months in advance through Recreation.gov. 
  • Backpackers along the Boy Scout Trail must camp in one of 14 designated campsites.   
  • Camping in other zones is 'at large' and visitors may choose their own low-impact site. 'At large' camping must be 1 mile from any Backcountry Trailhead, 1/2 mile from a legally open road, and 200 feet off a trail.   
  • Camping in or near rock shelters or in designated “day-use only” areas is strictly prohibited.
description.tertiary_page:
General Information:

Joshua Tree National Park is divided into 13 Backcountry Camping Zones. These zones do not have limits on advanced registration, but for same day registration, quotas apply. A complete list of Backpacking Zones and Backcountry Trailheads are listed below. As overnight parking is only permitted at one of the 13 backcountry trailheads, entry / exit points listed during the check-out process should match one of these trailheads, unless entering from outside of the park. Please note, not all zones (i.e. Maze Loop and East Zone) have a backcountry trailheads associated with them and are only accessible from outside the park boundary or by traveling through another zone.  

If you wish to enter and / or exit from outside of the park (i.e. entering the East Zone from CA-62 or CA-177), please select "Parking outside the park" as your entry/exit points. Please contact public lands agencies responsible for those areas regarding local regulations and restrictions (e.g. BLM Palm Springs - South Coast Field Office , BLM Barstow Field Office , .

Same Day Quotas per Zone:

  • There is no quota of same day permits per backpacking zone, regardless of whether or not those permits are obtained online or through the Joshua Tree National Park permitting office. However, if permiting begins to fill beyond two (2) same day permits issued, zones are subject to closing early. In order to ensure that you get your desired itinerary, it is best to book at least 24 hours in advance of your desired departure date.
  • Online, through recreation.gov, same day permits will be available up until 2pm on the day of departure. In person permits will be available up until 4pm through the Joshua Tree National Park permitting office, but may be subject to change based on demand and staff availability. 

Wilderness Backpacking Zones:

  • Black Rock
  • Covington
  • Quail Wash
  • Maze Loop
  • Juniper Flats
  • Lost Horse
  • Pine City
  • North Entrance
  • Twin Tanks
  • Pleasant Valley
  • Hexie Mountains
  • Pinto Mountains
  • Eagle Mountains
  • East Zone 

Entry/Exit Points: Backcountry Trailheads: (parking locations)

  • Black Rock Canyon
  • Geology Tour Road
  • Boy Scout Trailhead/ Key's West
  • Pleasant Valley
  • Twin Tanks
  • Cottonwood Springs
  • Indian Cove
  • North Entrance
  • Porcupine Wash
  • Covington Flats
  • Juniper Flats
  • Pine City
  • Turkey Flats

How to Book a two-night trip along the California Hiking and Riding Trail: 

Select a zone on either the west or east side of the park of where you intend to camp the first night. Options might include Black Rock, Covington, North Entrance, or Twin Tanks. Select a zone of where you might camp the second night. Options might be: Lost Horse, Twin Tanks, Covington, Black Rock, or Juniper Flats. At check-out, your entry point will either be Black Rock Backcountry Trailhead or North Entrance Backcountry Trailhead if you are intending to hike the entire trail. Your exit point will either be Black Rock Backcountry Trailhead or North Entrance based on your exiting location.

Note on combining the Boy Scout Trail Zone with other Zones:

It is possible to reserve a combination of sites along the Boy Scout Trail with "at-large" camping in other zones. For a trip starting with a single night on the Boy Scout Trail before continuing onto the Maze / Window Loops along the Big Pine Trail, the permitee would book their first night at one of the sites along the Boy Scout Trail and their second night in the Maze Zone. The online permitting process places no restrictions on camping reservations based on distance (i.e. non-adjoining zones) or topography, so please do not assume a trip is feasible because it can be booked online. Please research your planned route thoroughly before commiting to a reservation.

4675329001.description:
There is no at-large camping in Boy Scout Trail zone . Permittees must choose a designated site to camp in. Each site is unique and has a group-size limit and accommodates a varying amount of tents. Campsites are categorized into three sizes:

Small: 1-2 tents, 4 people maximum. Small sites include 1, 6, 9, 10, 13, and 14.

Medium: 3-4 tents, 7 people maximum. Medium sites include 2, 3, 4, 5, and 11.

Large: 5-8 tents, 12 people maximum. Large sites include 7, 8, and 12.

If you are a small group, please look for small or medium-sized sites first before booking a large site. There are signs on the trail directing backpackers to their designated sites. Backpackers must comply with the rules and regulations on the sign at their campsite.

4675329019.description: The Black Rock Zone features a wide variety of hiking trails through mountains, washes, ravines, and valleys. It has great views from the high peaks and ridges and provides habitat for large Joshua trees, pinyon pine, and juniper. With higher elevations of 4,000 - 5,500 feet, this zone offers cooler temperatures than most zones. During the colder months, freezing temperatures are common.

description_map.need_to_know:
The Black Rock Zone features hiking trails through mountains, washes, and valleys. It has great views of high peaks and can see Joshua trees, pinyon pine, and juniper. With elevations of 4,000 - 5,500 ft, this zone offers cooler temperatures than most zones. Prepare for freezing temperatures in colder months.

Trails: This zone offers options for loop hikes. Popular hiking trails include the Panorama Loop (6 miles round-trip), the West Side Loop (5 miles round-trip), Eureka Peak (20 miles round-trip), and CA Hiking and Riding Trail (37 miles one-way). Other trails include Burnt Hill, the Canyon View Loop, and Fault Line trail.

Bordering Zones: Covington 

Closest Backcountry Trailhead to Enter/Exit: Black Rock Backcountry Trailhead (4,000')

4675329019.name: Black Rock Zone

4675329020.description: The Covington Zone offers relatively easy access to some of the highest elevations ranging from 4,800 to ~5,600 feet. It features high peaks, scenic overlooks, and open valleys with some of the largest Joshua trees, pinyon pines, and junipers in the park. During the colder months, freezing temperatures are common.

description_map.need_to_know:
The Covington Zone offers relatively easy access to some of the highest elevations ranging from 4,800 to ~5,600 feet. It features high peaks, overlooks, and valleys with some of the largest Joshua trees, pinyon pines, and junipers in the park. Prepare for freezing temperatures in colder months.

Trails: Covington Crest and the CA Hiking and Riding Trail. Quail Mountain (5813’) is a popular destination; there is no maintained trail to the summit and requires off-trail navigation skills.

Bordering Zones: Black Rock , Juniper Flats, and Quail Wash .

Closest Backcountry Trailheads to Enter/Exit: Covington Flat (4800’), Black Rock (4,000'), and Juniper Flats (4,340’). To reach the Covington Flats trailhead, a 4-wheel drive vehicle is recommended.

4675329020.name: Covington Zone

4675329021.description: The Eagle Mountains Zone features rugged mountains, rocky canyons, and palm oases. It is among the warmer and lower elevation zones in the park. This region also includes the Southern Coxcombs, an extremely rugged and remote region that can be accessed from CA-177. Due to sensitive resources, camping is not allowed at Lost Palms Oasis, Victory Palms, and most of Munsen Canyon.

description_map.need_to_know:

This region also includes the Southern Coxcombs, an extremely rugged and remote region that can be accessed from CA-177. Due to sensitive resources, camping is not allowed at Lost Palms Oasis, Victory Palms, and most of Munsen Canyon.

Trails: Lost Palms Oasis (7.5 miles one-way)

Bordering Zones: Hexie Mountains, Pinto Mountains , and the East Zone 

Closest Backcountry Trailhead to Enter/Exit: Cottonwood Spring (3,100')
description_map.site_details: Warning: There is one maintained trail in this zone. Review public land agency rules when parking outside of the park. No camping in day use areas which includes Lost Palms Oasis.

4675329021.name: Eagle Mountains Zone

4675329022.description: The East Zone is a remote and rugged area in the northeast part of the park. It contains the Coxcomb Mountains and much of the Pinto Basin. Elevations range from 1,200 feet in the Pinto Basin to 4,400+ feet in the Coxcombs. There are no roads or hiking trails. Backpackers entering this area should be well versed in off-trail travel and navigation.

description_map.need_to_know:

Elevations range from 1,200 feet in the Pinto Basin to 4,400+ feet in the Coxcombs. There are no roads or hiking trails. Backpackers entering this area should be well versed in off-trail travel and navigation.

Trails: There are no maintained trails in this zone.

Bordering Zones: Pinto Mountains and Eagle Mountains .

Closest Backcountry Trailheads to Enter/Exit: There are no parking lots or backcountry trailheads in this zone. Backpackers are responsible for knowing where they can legally park.

4675329022.name: East Zone

4675329023.description: The Hexie Mountain Zone is a remote and rugged zone in the south-central part of the park. It features the Hexie Mountains and Cottonwood Mountains. Points of interest include Fried Liver Wash, Ruby Lee Well, and Monument Mountain. Elevations range from ~1,700 fee in the Pinto Basin to 4,800+ feet on Monument Mountain. Backpackers entering this area should be well versed in off-trail travel and navigation.

description_map.need_to_know:

Points of interest include Fried Liver Wash, Ruby Lee Well, and Monument Mountain. Elevations range from ~1,700 fee in the Pinto Basin to 4,800+ feet on Monument Mountain. Backpackers entering this area should be well versed in off-trail travel and navigation.

Trails: There are no maintained trails in this zone.

Bordering Zones: Pinto Mountains , Pleasant Valley , and Eagle Mountains .

Closest Backcountry Trailhead to Enter/Exit: Turkey Flats (1,791’), Porcupine Wash (2450’), and Cottonwood (3,000’).
description_map.site_details: If you carry an emergency signaling device, know its operation, limitations, and frequency of failure to transmit. If you activate the emergency help function on the device, understand the consequences of what you may be asking of rescue personnel.

4675329023.name: Hexie Mountains Zone

4675329024.description: The Juniper Flats Zone offers some of the higher, cooler elevations ranging from ~4,400 to nearly 5,600 feet. It features open valleys, mountainous terrain, and panoramic views. During the colder months, freezing temperatures are common. Overnight camping is not allowed near Stubbe Springs due to sensitive resources.

description_map.need_to_know:
The Juniper Flats Zone offers some of the higher, cooler elevations ranging from ~4,400 to nearly 5,600 feet. It features open valleys, mountainous terrain, and panoramic views. During the colder months, freezing temperatures are common. Overnight camping is not allowed near Stubbe Springs due to sensitive resources.

Trails: The Stubbe Springs Loop (12 miles round-trip) and the California Hiking and Riding Trail.

Bordering Zones: Covington , Quail Wash , and Lost Horse .

Closest Backcountry Trailheads to Enter/Exit: Juniper Flats (4,340’) and Covington Flats (4800’). To reach the Covington Flats trailhead, a 4-wheel drive vehicle is recommended.
description_map.site_details:
Overnight camping is not allowed near Stubbe Springs due to sensitive resources. 
Backpacking must take place, one mile from backcountry trailhead, at least a half mile from legally open roads, and at least 200 feet from designated trails.

4675329024.name: Juniper Flats Zone

4675329025.description: The Lost Horse Zone features rocky mountains, historical sites, and open valleys filled with Joshua trees, rock islands, and sandy washes. Elevations range from 3,500 to 5,300 feet. Camping is not allowed near any mining or historical sites.

description_map.need_to_know:
The Lost Horse Zone features rocky mountains, historical sites, and open valleys filled with Joshua trees, rock islands, and sandy washes. Elevations range from 3,500 to 5,300 feet. Camping is not allowed near any mining or historical sites.

Trails: The California Hiking and Riding Trail, Lost Horse Loop (6.5-mile loop), Big Trees Trail a.k.a. Lost Horse Connector Trail (3 miles one-way), and the Paac Kü̱vü̱hü̱’k trail (4.5 miles one-way).

Bordering Zones: Juniper Flats , Pleasant Valley , and Twin Tanks 

Closest Backcountry Trailheads to Enter/Exit: Juniper Flats (4,340’), Geology Tour (4,485’)
description_map.site_details: Backpacking must take place, one mile from backcountry trailhead, at least a half mile from legally open roads, and at least 200 feet from designated trails.

4675329025.name: Lost Horse Zone

4675329026.description: The North Entrance Zone is a small zone broken into two sections. One section is near the North Entrance Station in Twentynine Palms. The other section is east of the Twin Tanks campground. This zone features open valleys, sandy washes, and rugged mountains. Elevations range from 2,800 to 4,000+ feet.

description_map.need_to_know:
The North Entrance Zone is a small zone broken into two sections. One section is near the North Entrance Station in Twentynine Palms. The other section is east of the Twin Tanks campground. This zone features open valleys, sandy washes, and rugged mountains. Elevations range from 2,800 to 4,000+ feet.

Trails: California Hiking and Riding Trail (37 miles one-way)

Bordering Zones: Pinto Mountains , Twin Tanks , and Pine City . To the east, most of the zone is bordered by land managed by the Bureau of Land Management.

Closest Backcountry Trailheads to Enter/Exit: North Entrance (2,880') and Twin Tanks (3,900')

4675329026.name: North Entrance Zone

4675329027.description: The Pine City Zone is a small zone southeast of Queen Mountain. The zone includes open valleys, rugged mountains, and sandy washes cutting through rocky canyons. Elevations range from 4,000 to 4,800 feet. There are a limited number of permits available for this zone due to the popularity of the pine city area and it's limited number of campsites. Camping is not allowed at cultural or historic sites.

description_map.need_to_know:
The Pine City Zone is a small zone southeast of Queen Mountain. The zone includes open valleys, rugged mountains, and sandy washes cutting through rocky canyons. Elevations range from 4,000 to 4,800 feet. There are a limited number of permits available for this zone due to the popularity of the pine city area and it's limited number of campsites. Camping is not allowed at cultural or historic sites.

Trails: Pine City (1.5 miles one-way)

Bordering Zones: Twin Tanks and Lost Horse . North of the pine city zone is the Wonderland of Rocks, a day-use area where overnight camping is not allowed.

Closest Backcountry Trailheads to Enter/Exit: Pine City (4,440')
description_map.site_details: The camping in this zone is very restricted. Please avoid camping in rock shelters. Camping in the Wonderland of Rocks is prohibited.

4675329027.name: Pine City Zone

4675329028.description: The Pinto Mountains Zone is a rugged zone in the central part of the park. Points of interest include Pinto Mountain and the sand dunes along it's southern base. This zone is among the warmer and lower elevation zones in the park. There are no roads or hiking trails. Backpackers entering this area should be well versed in off-trail travel and navigation.

description_map.need_to_know:
The Pinto Mountains Zone is a rugged zone in the central part of the park. Points of interest include Pinto Mountain and the sand dunes along it's southern base. This zone is among the warmer and lower elevation zones in the park. There are no roads or hiking trails. Backpackers entering this area should be well versed in off-trail travel and navigation.

Trails: There are no maintained trails in this zone.

Bordering Zones: The Hexie Mountains and the East Zone . North of this zone is land managed by the Bureau of Land Management.

Closest Backcountry Trailheads to Enter/Exit: Turkey Flats (1,791') and Porcupine Wash (2450’)

4675329028.name: Pinto Mountains Zone

4675329029.description: The Pleasant Valley Zone occupies part of the transition zone between the Mojave and Colorado Deserts. While Pleasant Valley itself is generally open and flat, the southern half of this zone contains the little San Bernardino Mountains and Pushwalla Peak, rising to over 5000’ in elevation. Points of interest include Hexahedron Mine and Fried Liver Wash. Elevations range from 3,000 - 5,000+ feet.

description_map.need_to_know:
The Pleasant Valley Zone occupies part of the transition zone between the Mojave and Colorado Deserts. While Pleasant Valley itself is generally open and flat, the southern half of this zone contains the little San Bernardino Mountains and Pushwalla Peak, rising to over 5000’ in elevation. Points of interest include Hexahedron Mine and Fried Liver Wash. Elevations range from 3,000 - 5,000+ feet.

Trails: There are no maintained trails in this zone.

Bordering Zones: Hexie Mountains, Twin Tanks , and Lost Horse .

Closest Backcountry Trailheads to Enter/Exit: Pleasant Valley (3280’) and Turkey Flats (1791’). If accessing Pleasant Valley on Geology Tour Road, a high clearance, 4-wheel drive vehicle is recommended.

4675329029.name: Pleasant Valley Zone

4675329030.description: The Quail Wash Zone features open valleys, rocky canyons, and two of the highest peaks in the park—Quail Mountain (5,813') and Mount Minerva Hoyt (5,405'). This zone offers multi-day loop options when connecting to trails in the surrounding zones. Elevations range from ~3,400 to 5,813 feet. Camping is not allowed near Samuelson Rocks or in Smithwater Canyon due to sensitive resources.

description_map.need_to_know:
The Quail Wash Zone features open valleys, rocky canyons, and the highest peaks in the park—Quail Mountain (5,813') and Mt. Minerva Hoyt (5,405'). This zone offers multi-day loop options when connecting trails in the surrounding zones. Camping is not allowed near Samuelson Rocks or in Smithwater Canyon due to sensitive resources. 

Trails: The Bigfoot Trail, the Panorama Trail, and Johnnie Lang Connector Trail. Quail Mountain and Mt. Minerva Hoyt are popular destinations; however, there are no maintained trails to the summits and they require off-trail navigation skills.

Bordering Zones: Juniper Flats and Covington 

Closest Backcountry Trailheads to Enter/Exit: Boy Scout (4,000'), Covington Flats (4,800'), and Juniper Flats (4,340')
description_map.site_details: Camping is not allowed near Samuelson Rocks or in Smithwater Canyon due to sensitive resources.

4675329030.name: Quail Wash Zone

4675329031.description: The Maze Zone offers a variety of trails to choose from and features sandy washes, rocky ridgetops, and sweeping landscape views. This zone offers multi-day loop options when connecting to trails in the surrounding zones. Elevations range from ~3,000 to 4,200+ feet.

description_map.need_to_know:
The Maze Zone offers a variety of trails to choose from and features sandy washes, rocky ridgetops, and sweeping landscape views. This zone offers multi-day loop options when connecting to trails in the surrounding zones. Elevations range from ~3,000 to 4,200+ feet.

Trails: The North View Loop (4.5 miles), the Maze Loop (5 miles), the Window Loop (1.8 miles), the Big Pine Trail (1.6 miles one-way), the Burro/Rocky View Loop (4.5 miles), and the North Canyon Trail (1.6 miles one-way).

Bordering Zones: The Boy Scout Trail and Quail Wash 

Closest Backcountry Trailheads to Enter/Exit: Boy Scout (4,000') and Indian Cove (2,800')
description_map.site_details: Parking within the park for backpacking is restricted to backcountry trailheads. In order to camp in this zone, you must park at either the Boy Scout Trailhead, Indian Cove Trailhead, or outside the park.

4675329031.name: The Maze Zone

4675329032.description: The Twin Tanks Zone is on the eastern edge of the Mojave Desert section of the park and features open valleys, panoramic views, and a portion of the Hexie Mountains. Points of interest include Crown Prince Lookout, Twin Tanks, and Stirrup Tank. Elevations range from ~3,500 to 4,500 feet.

description_map.need_to_know:
The Twin Tanks Zone is on the eastern edge of the Mojave Desert section of the park and features open valleys, and views of the Hexie Mountains. Points of interest include Crown Prince Lookout, Twin Tanks, and Stirrup Tank. Elevations range from ~3,500 to 4,500 feet.

Trails: The California Hiking and Riding Trail. Most of the social trails leading west from the Twin Tanks backcountry trailhead do not take you one mile from the trailhead. You must be one mile away from the trailhead to legally camp. Camping near the Twin Tanks is discouraged due to sensitive resources.

Bordering Zones: Lost Horse , Pleasant Valley , and North Entrance .

Closest Backcountry Trailheads to Enter/Exit: Twin Tanks (3,900') and Geology Tour Road (4,485’)
description_map.site_details: Please note that most of the social trails leading west from the Twin Tanks backcountry trailhead do not take you one mile from the trailhead. You must be one mile away from the trailhead to legally camp. Camping near the Twin Tanks is discouraged due to sensitive resources.

4675329032.name: Twin Tanks Zone
